artifact.title: KT Cloud Expands South Korea’s AI Infrastructure With a Planned 110 MW Data Center Campus
artifact.content:
South Korea’s AI infrastructure expansion has reached a new commercial milestone. Singapore-based Keppel confirmed that KT Cloud has committed to the full capacity of a planned 60 MW data center in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province. Announced November 26, 2026, the agreement connects the development with KT Cloud’s separate 50 MW Ansan facility, creating a planned two-site cluster with 110 MW of combined electrical capacity.

A new lease anchors the second development

According to Keppel’s announcement, the fund acquired the development site in June and has secured construction permits and power approvals. Construction is scheduled to begin in November 2026, with service targeted for 2030. The commitment covers the facility’s entire capacity, but leasing capacity does not mean that servers are installed or electricity is being consumed.

The second facility will occupy approximately 52,622 square meters of gross floor area across eight above-ground levels and two basement levels. ChosunBiz reports that the buildings will be approximately 2.5 kilometers apart. The original 50 MW development broke ground in October, according to Data Center Dynamics, and is expected to enter service in 2029.

Gross power is not GPU power

Keppel describes the new development’s 60 MW figure as gross electrical capacity. Transformers, uninterruptible power supplies, cooling pumps, fans and other infrastructure all draw electricity or introduce conversion losses. Consequently, the amount of power available to computing equipment will be lower than the facility’s gross capacity.

For illustration, a facility drawing 60 MW at a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.20 would have an IT power budget of 50 MW, calculated as 60 ÷ 1.20. Continuous operation at the full 60 MW would consume 525,600 MWh over a 365-day year. Neither assumption represents measured operating performance or a disclosed electricity-consumption forecast for Ansan.

Cooling and networking determine usable capacity

KT Cloud plans liquid-cooling infrastructure on each floor. In a direct-to-chip system, cold plates carry heat away from processors into circulating coolant. Coolant distribution units exchange heat between server and facility loops, while external heat-rejection equipment ultimately transfers thermal energy to the environment. Pump redundancy, pressure management, leak detection and maintenance isolation become essential operating considerations, as explained in our CDU redundancy lesson.

A two-site campus also creates opportunities for phased expansion and geographic separation of infrastructure. Optical links can connect facilities for data transfer and service replication, but the project’s interconnection topology, bandwidth, accelerator inventory and workload allocation have not been disclosed. Distributed AI training performance depends on network latency and communication throughput, not simply aggregate electrical capacity.

Keppel says the new facility will be designed to Tier III-equivalent specifications. That describes the intended resilience standard rather than evidence of completed independent certification. Similar distinctions between commitments and commissioned capacity appear in our coverage of Bitdeer’s 300 MW Ohio proposal, its 121 MW Norwegian conversion and Soluna’s Texas solar-adjacent campus.

KT Group’s stated objective is to offer 1 GW of AI data center capacity by 2031. Ansan’s combined planned capacity represents 11% of that target on a nominal MW basis, without establishing whether the group uses identical measurement boundaries throughout its portfolio. The milestones worth watching are construction progress, electrical commissioning, thermal-system testing and the actual start of customer service.
